title: The Machine That Can Stand Still in the Sky
blurb: A helicopter carries its own wind. Its wings spin, so it never has to move forward to stay up.

blocks.prompt: Wings That Spin
blocks.text: A helicopter has wings, but they do not sit still. They spin. Each blade on top is a long thin wing. When the blades whirl around, they push air down, and that push lifts the helicopter straight up. That is why a helicopter does not need a runway. It can lift off from a field, a roof, or a ship at sea. It can hover, which means it stays in one spot in the air. Now look at the small propeller on the tail. Without it, the whole helicopter would spin in circles.

blocks.prompt: Why Helicopters Have a Little Propeller on the Tail
blocks.text: An airplane wing has to move fast through the air to make lift, and that is why planes need long runways. A helicopter solves the problem a different way. Instead of dragging its wings through the air, it spins them. The blades on top are wings, and they whirl around a few hundred times every minute. They push air down. The air pushes back. Up goes the helicopter, no runway needed. But spinning those heavy blades creates a problem. The engine turns the blades one way, and the machinery tries to twist the body of the helicopter the other way. Left alone, the cabin would spin like a top with the pilot inside it. That is the job of the little propeller on the tail. It faces sideways and blows air out to one side, and that steady push holds the body straight. The pilot presses foot pedals to make the tail rotor push harder or softer. Push harder and the nose swings one way. Ease off and it swings back.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Collective: the lever that makes every blade bite harder
Cyclic: the stick that tilts the whole spinning disc
Pedals: they control the tail rotor and swing the nose
Autorotation: how a pilot lands with a dead engine
A helicopter flies wherever its rotor disc points

blocks.prompt: Flying a Helicopter Takes Both Hands and Both Feet
blocks.text: A helicopter pilot has three controls working at once, and none of them can be ignored for long. In the pilot's left hand is the collective, a lever that looks a bit like a parking brake. Pulling it up changes the angle of every rotor blade at the same time, so all of them bite harder into the air. More bite means more lift, and the helicopter climbs. Push the collective down and it sinks. In the right hand is the cyclic, a stick between the knees. This one is clever. It changes the angle of each blade depending on where that blade is in its circle. The result is that the whole spinning disc of blades tilts, like a dinner plate tipping. Tilt it forward and the helicopter flies forward. Tilt it left and it slides left. A helicopter goes wherever its rotor disc points. Under the pilot's feet are the pedals, which control the tail rotor and swing the nose left or right. Now here is the part people get wrong. If the engine quits, a helicopter does not drop like a stone. The pilot immediately pushes the collective all the way down. The helicopter starts falling, and the air rushing up through the rotor keeps the blades spinning, the way wind keeps a pinwheel turning. Those free spinning blades store energy. Near the ground the pilot pulls the collective back up, trades that stored energy for one last cushion of lift, and sets the machine down. The move is called autorotation, and every helicopter pilot practices it before ever flying alone.

blocks.prompt: The Slowest Fast Machine
blocks.text: The word helicopter is stitched together from two Greek pieces: helix, meaning spiral, and pteron, meaning wing. A French inventor put them together in 1861, nearly fifty years before anyone built a machine worth the name. The idea is much older. Around 1480 Leonardo da Vinci sketched an aerial screw, a spiral canopy meant to bore upward through the air. It would never have flown. He had no engine light enough, and the whole machine would simply have spun beneath its own screw. Chinese children had been spinning bamboo flying tops for well over a thousand years, and those actually worked, which was the more useful clue. Real progress waited on engines. In 1909 a young Russian named Igor Sikorsky built a helicopter that could not lift its own weight. He built a second one. It failed too. He gave up, spent thirty years building airplanes instead, and came back. In 1939 his VS-300 rose off a field in Connecticut, tethered by ropes, with Sikorsky at the controls in a business suit and a fedora hat. One big rotor on top, one small rotor on the tail. Nearly every helicopter since has copied that layout. But the design carries a built in speed limit, and it is worth understanding. Think of the rotor as a spinning wheel of wings. When the helicopter flies forward, the blade sweeping around on one side is traveling in the same direction as the aircraft, so it meets the air very fast. Half a turn later that same blade is sweeping the other way, against the direction of travel, and its speed through the air is now the rotor speed minus the aircraft speed. Fly fast enough and the retreating blade slows so much that it stops making lift. The helicopter tries to roll over. That is why a machine that can hover motionless over a rooftop struggles to outrun a car on the highway. The world speed record for a conventional helicopter, set by a modified Westland Lynx in 1986, is about 249 miles per hour, and it has stood ever since.

blocks.prompt: Read the passage, then work through each part.

notes: Torque: spin the rotor one way, the body wants to spin the other
The tail rotor burns roughly a tenth of the engine's power
Retreating blade stall caps conventional helicopter speed
Autorotation turns a falling helicopter into a windmill
2005: an AS350 landed on the summit of Everest
2021: Ingenuity flew on Mars in one percent of Earth's air

blocks.prompt: Beating the Air Into Submission
blocks.text: There is an old joke among pilots that airplanes fly, while helicopters merely beat the air into submission. It is a slander with a grain of truth in it. An airplane is a fundamentally lazy machine: throw it forward and the fixed wings do the work. A helicopter has no such luxury. It carries its own wind. The rotor overhead is a set of wings on a leash, whipped around a mast a few hundred times a minute so that they never stop meeting fresh air. The moment that spinning stops, the wings stop being wings. This buys the helicopter the one thing no fixed wing aircraft can have: the ability to stay. An airplane must keep moving or fall. A helicopter can hold a position over a sinking trawler, a burning roof, a canyon ledge, or a stretcher on a highway, and hold it while people are pulled aboard. Almost every job helicopters do well comes from that single ability, and almost every job they do badly comes from the price they pay for it. The price begins with torque. Spin a heavy rotor one way and Newton's third law insists the body try to spin the other. The fix that Igor Sikorsky settled on in 1939, and that the industry has largely used ever since, is a small propeller mounted sideways on the tail. It does not push the helicopter forward. It pushes against the twist, all day, burning perhaps a tenth of the engine's power to accomplish nothing except keeping the cabin pointed where the pilot wants it. The next price is speed. In forward flight the advancing blade meets the air at rotor speed plus airspeed, while the retreating blade meets it at rotor speed minus airspeed. Push the aircraft faster and the two halves of the disc grow more and more unequal: the advancing tip creeps toward the speed of sound while the retreating blade runs out of airflow and stalls. That imbalance is why the record for a conventional helicopter, set by a modified Westland Lynx in 1986, sits at roughly 249 miles per hour, and why nobody has beaten it in forty years. The engines have improved. The physics has not changed. The third price is that when the engine stops, the pilot has seconds, not minutes. But here the design quietly redeems itself. Drop the collective and the falling helicopter becomes a windmill: air rushing up through the disc keeps the blades turning, storing energy in their spinning mass. Near the ground the pilot cashes that energy in, flaring the disc and pulling the collective to buy a last few feet of lift. The maneuver is called autorotation, and student pilots practice it long before they are trusted to fly alone. For all its compromises, the layout is astonishingly capable. In 2005 a test pilot named Didier Delsalle set an AS350 down on the summit of Everest, at 29,029 feet, in air roughly a third as thick as the air at sea level. In 2021 a four pound machine called Ingenuity lifted off the floor of Jezero Crater on Mars, where the atmosphere is about one percent of Earth's. To find any grip at all its blades had to spin near 2,500 revolutions per minute, roughly five times faster than a helicopter's on Earth. It was built to make five flights. It made 72. Beating the air into submission, it turns out, is a strategy that travels.
